findings.requirement_type: Program — 90-Day Cancellation Notice Benchmark (Cross-Program)
findings.contract_quote: RMF General §1: '90-day notice of cancellation is the broker benchmark... Anything less than the contract requirement is a Bad or Ugly finding... The broker target is 90 days.'
findings.policy_quote: E&O (Gemini): 60 days for-cause / 10 days nonpayment. Convex: follows form. Cyber (AmTrust): not visible in extracted excerpt.
findings.policy_page: Gemini page 15; Convex follows form; AmTrust not visible
findings.gap_description: Sacramento §VI.A.2 places notification obligation on the Contractor (10-day renewal evidence + immediate notice of carrier comm) — does not require a 30+ day Designated Entity NOC. Maricopa §8.2.15 requires 30-day cancellation/material-change notice direct from carrier. Best practice broker target is 90 days. Across the program: E&O 60-day base meets Maricopa but not the 90-day benchmark; Cyber not visible; CGL/Auto/WC/Umbrella not in audit batch.
findings.plain_english: The broker industry best-practice is 90 days' notice if the carrier is going to cancel or materially change a policy. Maricopa requires at least 30 days. Your E&O is at 60 days (meets Maricopa, falls short of broker best practice). The Cyber and other policies need to be verified.
findings.recommendation: At each renewal, request 90-day Designated Entity NOC across all program policies (Hanover Designated Entity NOC endorsement 401-1235 is a known available form for Hanover lines per KB knowledge). Specifically pursue this on CGL, Auto, Umbrella, WC, and Cyber. E&O 60 days is acceptable but ask Gemini for 90.

findings.requirement_type: Program — Notice & Knowledge Cross-Program (Officer-Limited Endorsement)
findings.contract_quote: RMF General §4: 'Is the policy endorsed so that a covered occurrence is only triggered when the company's officer, the person responsible for insurance, the risk manager, or equivalent is notified — rather than ANY employee's knowledge being imputed to the entity?'
findings.policy_quote: E&O: confirmed officer-limited (CEO/CFO/GC/RM) per End. #3. Cyber: not visible. CGL/Auto/WC: not in audit batch.
findings.gap_description: Notice & Knowledge officer-limitation is confirmed only on E&O. Need verification across Cyber, CGL, Auto, WC, Mgmt Liability, and Umbrella. Without this endorsement, a low-level employee's awareness of an incident can be imputed to the entity for notice purposes — voiding coverage if not formally reported up.
findings.plain_english: Best practice is to make sure NO policy can use a low-level employee's awareness of an incident to deny coverage. Your E&O has this fix in place. We need to confirm it's also on the Cyber, CGL, Auto, Workers' Comp, and Management Liability policies — historically the most commonly missed RMF item.
findings.recommendation: Confirm officer-limited Notice & Knowledge endorsement on every program policy (or 'Knowledge of Occurrence' / 'Notice Manager' carrier-equivalents). Where missing, add at next available endorsement window (most carriers add this at no charge).

findings.requirement_type: Program — Unintentional Errors and Omissions Giveback (Cross-Program)
findings.contract_quote: RMF General §2: 'Does the policy include an Unintentional Errors and Omissions giveback (often endorsed for GL — sometimes embedded in package forms)? Without it, an inadvertent failure to report a location, vehicle, or operation can result in coverage denial.'
findings.policy_quote: Not visible across the policies in this audit batch (E&O, Convex, Cyber).
findings.gap_description: Unintentional E&O giveback is most common on CGL and Property (sometimes Crime and Cyber). With three Runbeck legal entities in the program (Runbeck Election Services LLC, Runbeck Properties LLC, Runbeck Investments LLC, Runbeck Graphics Inc) and 31 states of operation, the risk of inadvertently failing to schedule a location, entity, or operation is real. Without this giveback, inadvertent omissions can void coverage.
findings.plain_english: If your team accidentally forgets to add a new location, vehicle, or operation to a policy, the Unintentional E&O endorsement protects you from the carrier denying coverage on that basis. With 31 states of operations and four legal entities, inadvertent omissions are a real risk. We should make sure this is endorsed on every applicable policy.
findings.recommendation: When the CGL, Auto, and Property policies are received for full audit, confirm Unintentional E&O giveback (carrier-specific endorsement names vary). If absent, add at next renewal — typically at no or nominal cost.

findings.requirement_type: Program — Blanket Waiver of Subrogation (Cross-Program)
findings.contract_quote: The policies required hereunder, except Workers' Compensation and Errors and Omissions, shall contain a waiver of transfer of rights of recovery (subrogation) against County, its agents, representatives, officers, directors, officials, and employees... (Maricopa §8.2.8 and §8.2.12 for WC) ... Workers' Compensation Waiver of Subrogation: ... shall be endorsed to state that the workers' compensation carrier waives its right of subrogation against the COUNTY... (Sacramento §VIII)
findings.contract_file: Sacramento County and Maricopa County Insurance Requirements
findings.policy_quote: Cyber: not visible. E&O: not required (carved out). CGL/Auto/WC/Umbrella: not in audit batch.
findings.gap_description: Both Sacramento and Maricopa require blanket Waiver of Subrogation across CGL, Auto, WC, Cyber (Maricopa), and Umbrella. CA WC requires WC 04 03 06 specifically (separate premium). Need to verify across program: E&O is correctly carved out, but every other line must have blanket WoS.
findings.plain_english: Both counties require your insurers to waive their right to come after the County after paying a claim. Across CGL, Auto, WC, Cyber, and Umbrella, this should be blanket (any party where required by written contract). For California WC specifically there's a separate endorsement (WC 04 03 06) that costs extra — verify it's in place for any work performed in CA.
findings.recommendation: On full program audit, verify blanket WoS on each applicable policy. For CA WC specifically, confirm WC 04 03 06 is endorsed AND that California is on Item 3.A of the WC information page.

findings.requirement_type: Program — Named Insured Asymmetry Across Policies
findings.contract_quote: RMF General §3: 'For each policy, capture the full Named Insured + Additional Named Insured list. Compare across the program — if an entity (subsidiary, JV, holding company, real-estate LLC, 401(k) plan) appears on some policies but not others, flag the asymmetry.'
findings.policy_quote: Cyber lists 4 entities (Runbeck Election Services LLC, Runbeck Properties LLC, Runbeck Investments LLC, Runbeck Graphics Inc). E&O primary lists 2 (Runbeck Election Services Inc + Runbeck Graphics Inc via End. #13). Convex Excess lists 1 (Runbeck Election Services LLC).
findings.gap_description: Significant Named Insured asymmetry across the three audited policies. Runbeck Properties LLC and Runbeck Investments LLC are named on Cyber but missing from E&O and Convex. The Cyber correctly reflects the 4-entity structure post-Policy Change #1. The E&O still uses 'Inc' entity-type and only adds Runbeck Graphics; the Convex names only Runbeck Election Services LLC. Risk: Runbeck Properties (likely real-estate holder) and Runbeck Investments (likely PE/holding entity) have no E&O coverage if a claim arose against them, and reverse — claims against the LLC may be denied on the E&O if the named entity is 'Inc.'
findings.plain_english: The four Runbeck entities are on the Cyber policy but not consistently on the E&O. Runbeck Properties and Runbeck Investments — likely the real-estate and holding entities — have no E&O coverage at all. The 'Inc' vs 'LLC' naming inconsistency makes this worse: a claim against Runbeck Election Services LLC could be denied on a policy that names Runbeck Election Services Inc.
findings.recommendation: Use the Cyber Named Insured schedule as the authoritative template. Endorse all four entities onto E&O primary, Convex excess, and every other program policy (CGL, Auto, WC, Umbrella, Mgmt Liability). Confirm corporate counsel has identified all material entities (including any 401(k) plan, JV, or affiliates) and ensure each is appropriately scheduled. Typical cost: nominal endorsement fees only.
discoveryQuestions: What does Runbeck Properties LLC do, and does it have any operational or contractual exposure that should be covered by E&O?
What does Runbeck Investments LLC do — is it the PE-investor entity or an internal holding company?
If a claim were brought against Runbeck Investments LLC tomorrow, which policy would respond?
Has corporate counsel reviewed the Named Insured schedules across all policies for completeness?

findings.requirement_type: Program — Maricopa Indemnity Uncapped by Insurance Limits
findings.contract_quote: The amount and type of insurance coverage requirements set forth herein will in no way be construed as limiting the scope of the indemnity in this section.
findings.policy_quote: Insurance limits across program (per analyzed batch): E&O $10M tower (with split-limits caveat); Cyber $4M shared aggregate. Other lines not in audit batch.
findings.gap_description: Standard non-limitation clause — Run-Test's indemnification obligation to Maricopa is not capped at insurance limits. Liability above policy limits is uninsured exposure to balance sheet. With Cyber materially under-limited ($4M vs $5M required, with defense-within-limits erosion to ~$1M-$1.5M effective) and E&O subject to split-limits caps on pre-2019 acts, the residual balance-sheet exposure is meaningful — particularly for a PE-backed company where shareholder enterprise value is the asset at risk.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa's indemnification clause says insurance limits do NOT cap your obligation to pay them. So if you're liable for $20M, the Cyber's $4M and E&O's $10M won't end the conversation — Run-Test (and ultimately the PE sponsor) is on the hook for the rest. This is standard contract language but worth flagging given the gaps in your program.
findings.recommendation: Brief PE sponsor and CFO on residual uninsured exposure. Strengthen the program to reduce that exposure: (1) raise Cyber to $5M+ with stable aggregate (see Cyber findings); (2) fix E&O split limits (see finding-002); (3) consider increasing Umbrella limits if not already at $10M+. Indemnity won't change, but tower can.
discoveryQuestions: Has your PE sponsor been briefed on the residual uninsured exposure given Maricopa's uncapped indemnity language and the gaps in your Cyber and E&O programs?
How does Run-Test's enterprise valuation compare to the worst-case uninsured loss scenario from a major election-related lawsuit?

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento — Civil Code §2782 Carve-Out (Active Negligence)
findings.contract_quote: Coverage shall not extend to any indemnity coverage for the active negligence of the additional insured in any case where an agreement to indemnify the additional insured would be invalid under Subdivision (b) of Section 2782 of the Civil Code.
findings.policy_quote: California public policy limit — does not require a special endorsement; this is a contract-level acknowledgement.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento §VII.B is a CA public-policy compliance acknowledgment, not an insurance requirement. Cal. Civ. Code §2782(b) bars indemnification of a public agency for its own active negligence — Sacramento contractually accepts this limit. No endorsement action required on Run-Test policies.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento isn't asking your insurance to cover their own negligence — they're acknowledging that California law won't allow them to demand that. This is a contract-level safety net, not an insurance requirement.
findings.recommendation: No action required on insurance. Operations team should document the §2782(b) acknowledgment in contract files for clarity.

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento — Severability of Interest
findings.contract_quote: SEVERABILITY OF INTEREST: The CONTRACTOR's insurance shall apply separately to each insured against whom claim is made or suit is brought, except with respect to the limits of the insurer's liability.
findings.policy_quote: Standard ISO CG 0001 (assumed on Hanover CGL — not in audit batch) includes Separation of Insureds in §IV.7.
findings.gap_description: Separation of Insureds is standard ISO CG 00 01 §IV.7 language. Verify Hanover CGL uses CG 00 01 (vs proprietary form) when policy is provided for full audit; standard ISO form satisfies the requirement.
findings.plain_english: Standard CGL forms include this automatically — the policy covers each insured separately, so a claim by one insured against another doesn't prevent coverage. Should be a non-issue on a Hanover CGL using standard ISO forms.
findings.recommendation: Verify Hanover CGL is on ISO CG 00 01 base form (not proprietary) when policy is reviewed. If proprietary, confirm Separation of Insureds equivalent.

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento — Subcontractor Pass-Through Requirements
findings.contract_quote: SUBCONTRACTORS: CONTRACTOR shall be responsible for the acts and omissions of all its subcontractors and additional insured endorsements as provided by CONTRACTORs subcontractor.
findings.policy_quote: Subcontractor agreements not in audit batch.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento places responsibility on Run-Test for the acts and omissions of its subcontractors AND for ensuring those subs provide AI endorsements. Implied flow-down — Run-Test must include matching insurance requirements in its sub agreements. Need to verify Run-Test's subcontracting practices and standard sub-vendor insurance requirements.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento makes you responsible for what your subs do — and requires your subs to add the County as Additional Insured on their policies too. We need to confirm your subcontractor agreements actually require this from your subs (mail processors, IT consultants, equipment vendors, etc.) and that you collect their COIs and endorsements.
findings.recommendation: Audit Run-Test's standard subcontractor agreement for downstream insurance requirements that mirror Sacramento's. Implement (or strengthen) a sub-COI collection process — track that every active sub has provided current COIs naming Sacramento County (and other applicable counties) as AI on the sub's GL/Auto. Consider centralized contract-management software to track sub compliance.
discoveryQuestions: What types of subcontractors does Run-Test use — mail processors, IT, equipment maintenance, courier services?
Do your subcontractor agreements currently require Additional Insured status for your county clients?
Who at Run-Test owns the process of collecting and reviewing subcontractor COIs?

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa — Indemnification Comparative-Negligence Compatibility
findings.contract_quote: To the fullest extent permitted by law, and to the extent that claims, damages, losses, or expenses are not covered and paid by insurance purchased by the contractor, the contractor shall defend, indemnify, and hold harmless the County (as Owner)... but only to the extent caused by the negligent acts or omissions of the contractor, a subcontractor, anyone directly or indirectly employed by them, or anyone for whose acts they may be liable... The scope of this indemnification does not extend to the sole negligence of County.
findings.policy_quote: Indemnification scope is limited to extent of contractor negligence; AZ comparative negligence applies; sole-negligence carve-out for County.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa's indemnification clause is properly drafted under AZ A.R.S. §32-1159 and §34-226 — limited to extent of contractor negligence rather than unlimited or 'sole negligence' tied. Insurable contractual liability under standard CGL contractual liability coverage. No special endorsement required.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa's indemnification language is reasonably balanced — you're only on the hook to the extent your team (or subs) was negligent. Arizona's comparative-fault rules apply. This is the kind of clause your standard CGL contractual liability coverage handles, assuming the CGL has blanket contractual.
findings.recommendation: No action on contract scope. Verify CGL has blanket contractual liability (standard ISO CG 00 01 includes via the 'insured contract' definition) when CGL is audited.

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento — COI & Endorsement Copies Required Pre-Performance
findings.contract_quote: CONTRACTOR shall furnish the COUNTY with certificates evidencing coverage required below. Copies of required endorsements must be attached to provided certificates. ... All certificates, evidences of self-insurance, and additional insured endorsements are to be received and approved by the County before performance commences.
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement copies (not just COI references) must be attached and approved by County before performance.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento requires actual endorsement COPIES — not just COI references — to be attached and approved before performance commences. County also reserves right to require certified copies of policies. Process verification needed: confirm Run-Test's COI delivery to Sacramento includes copies of AI, WoS, P&NC, and Designated Entity NOC endorsements (where required), not just ACORD COI line items.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento doesn't accept just an ACORD certificate — they want actual copies of the endorsements showing them as Additional Insured, Waiver of Subrogation, etc. We need to confirm that whoever issued COIs to Sacramento attached the actual endorsement forms.
findings.recommendation: Pull Run-Test's most recent Sacramento County COI submissions and confirm endorsement copies were attached. Implement a checklist for Sacramento and similar high-bar counties (Maricopa) to ensure full endorsement packages travel with COIs going forward.

findings.requirement_type: Both Counties — 30-Day Claim Notice / 10-Day Lawsuit Notice Obligation
findings.contract_quote: If any claim for damages is filed with CONTRACTOR or if any lawsuit is instituted against CONTRACTOR, that arise out of or are in any way connected with CONTRACTOR's performance under this Agreement and that in any way, directly or indirectly, contingently or otherwise, affect or might reasonably affect COUNTY, CONTRACTOR shall give prompt and timely notice thereof to COUNTY. Notice shall be prompt and timely if given within thirty (30) days following the date of receipt of a claim or ten (10) days following the date of service of process of a lawsuit.
findings.policy_quote: Contractor's contractual notice duty to County: 30 days from claim receipt; 10 days from service of process. Independent of carrier notice obligations.
findings.gap_description: This is a Run-Test operational obligation, not an insurance endorsement. Need to verify that Run-Test's claims-management protocol includes this 30/10-day pass-through to county clients. Failing to notify within window is a contract breach independent of insurance coverage.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento expects to hear about any claim related to Run-Test's work for them within 30 days (or within 10 days of being served with a lawsuit). This isn't an insurance issue — it's an operational notification process. We need to make sure your claims-management workflow has Sacramento and any other county on the notification routing.
findings.recommendation: Document and implement a claims-incident protocol that includes county client notification within contractual timeframes. Maintain a list of every active county/government client and the specific notification address per contract. Review at each contract renewal.
discoveryQuestions: When you've received claims or lawsuits in the past, how did you handle notifying the affected county clients?
Is there a written incident-response protocol that maps each county's notification requirements?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Biometric Identifiers Coverage (BIPA-Style)
findings.contract_quote: [Cyber] policy shall include... invasion of privacy (regardless of the type of media involved in the loss of private information)...
findings.policy_quote: E&O End. #21 (VP 09 97 06 22) excludes biometric identifier statutory violations from E&O. Cyber policy biometric coverage scope not visible in extracted excerpt.
findings.gap_description: If Run-Test handles signature data, voiceprint authentication, fingerprint or other biometric data in any election authentication or voter-verification process, Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA-style) statutes in Illinois, Texas, Washington, and other states create regulatory and class-action exposure. E&O excludes biometric statutory claims; Cyber must cover or this is a true uninsured exposure.
findings.plain_english: If Run-Test ever processes signatures, voice prints, fingerprints, or any other biometric data — even just signature-verification on mail ballots — there are state laws (Illinois BIPA most famously) that create automatic statutory damages and class-action exposure. Your E&O specifically excludes this. We need to verify your Cyber policy actually covers it.
findings.recommendation: Pull full Cyber policy form. Specifically verify whether biometric statutory violations (BIPA, Texas CUBI, WA HB 1493, etc.) are covered, sublimited, or excluded. If excluded, this is a genuine coverage gap that needs resolution before any biometric-touching service line expands.
discoveryQuestions: Does Run-Test's signature-verification process for mail ballots involve any storage or processing of signature data?
Are you offering any biometric authentication services (fingerprint, voiceprint) to counties?
Have you operated in Illinois, Texas, or Washington — states with active biometric privacy statutes?

findings.requirement_type: General Liability — Policy Entirely Missing from Program
findings.contract_quote: Commercial General Liability (CGL) insurance ... with a limit of not less than $2,000,000 for each occurrence, $4,000,000 Products/Completed Operations Aggregate, and $4,000,000 General Aggregate Limit. The policy shall include coverage for premises liability, bodily injury, broad form property damage, personal injury, products and completed operations and blanket contractual coverage ... There shall be no endorsement or modifications of the CGL limiting the scope of coverage for liability arising from explosion, collapse, or underground property damage. (Maricopa §8.2.10) ... Building Trades General Aggregate: $2,000,000; Products Comp/Op Aggregate: $2,000,000; Personal & Adv. Injury: $1,000,000; Each Occurrence: $1,000,000; Fire Damage: $100,000. (Sacramento §III.A)
findings.contract_page: Maricopa §8.2.10 Pg 6 of 41; Sacramento §III.A Pg 2 of 4
findings.policy_quote: No General Liability policy was provided in this program audit submission. The only policies received were Hanover Workers' Compensation (WD4-H218283-06) and Hartford Twin City Management Liability (59 KB 0575120-24).
findings.gap_description: Both Sacramento County and Maricopa County contracts require Commercial General Liability coverage with specific limits, AI status, primary/noncontributory wording, blanket contractual liability, and (Maricopa) no XCU exclusions. No GL policy is present in the program submission. Without a CGL, virtually every premises-liability, products-liability, and operations-liability claim from any of the 31 states Run-Test serves is uninsured. This single gap voids compliance on Sacramento req-001, req-002, req-005 (in part), req-008, req-009, req-010, req-011, and Maricopa req-009, req-006, req-004, req-007.
findings.plain_english: Run-Test does not appear to have a General Liability policy on file with us. CGL is the foundation policy of any commercial insurance program — it covers premises slip-and-falls, bodily injury to third parties, products liability, and operations claims. A bodily injury or property damage claim from any county, vendor, voter, or visitor would have no coverage. Both your Sacramento and Maricopa contracts require this. Without it, every county contract you have is in technical breach and every claim is paid out of operating cash. This is the highest-priority item in the entire audit.
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether a GL policy exists and was simply not provided for review. If none exists, place a CGL immediately at $2M occurrence / $4M aggregate / $4M products-completed minimum (to satisfy Maricopa's higher tier). Ensure ISO CG 00 01 occurrence form, blanket contractual, blanket AI (CG 20 10 + CG 20 37), Primary & Noncontributory (CG 20 01), Blanket Waiver of Subrogation (CG 24 04), Per-Project Aggregate (CG 25 03 if any construction is performed), no XCU exclusion, and Notice/Knowledge endorsement limited to officer/risk manager.
discoveryQuestions: Walk me through the last time a member of the public — a voter, a visitor, a vendor — was injured at one of your facilities. Where did the bill go, and what would happen if it occurred today?

Your Sacramento contract requires a $1M/$2M GL with no added exclusions, and Maricopa requires $2M/$4M with explicit no-XCU language — when was the last time someone walked through every endorsement on your GL to make sure neither of those conditions is breached?
If a county sued you tomorrow because a defective ballot envelope caused mail delivery problems statewide, do you know which policy responds to the products liability claim — and at what limit?

findings.requirement_type: Commercial Auto — Policy Entirely Missing from Program
findings.contract_quote: Commercial/Business Automobile Liability insurance with a combined single limit ... of not less than $2,000,000 each occurrence with respect to any of the Contractor's owned, hired, and non-owned vehicles ... (Maricopa §8.2.11). Commercial Automobile Liability for Corporate/business owned vehicles including non-owned and hired, $1,000,000 Combined Single Limit. (Sacramento §III.B)
findings.contract_page: Maricopa §8.2.11 Pg 6 of 41; Sacramento §III.B Pg 2 of 4
findings.policy_quote: No Commercial Auto policy was provided in this program audit submission.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test transports ballots, election technology, and printing materials to county sites across 31 states. Auto exposure is inherent to the business — owned trucks, hired delivery vehicles, employees driving personal vehicles on company errands. No Commercial Auto policy is in this submission. Both contracts require $1M-$2M CSL covering owned/hired/non-owned vehicles. Without an Auto policy: any vehicle accident causing third-party injury or property damage during election logistics is uninsured beyond personal coverage that almost certainly excludes business use. Hired/Non-Owned Auto Liability and Hired Auto Physical Damage both fail.
findings.plain_english: We don't have an Auto policy on file. Election services means you're moving ballots, mail, and equipment to courthouses and post offices constantly — by truck, by employee car, by hired carrier. If an employee on a courthouse run rear-ends a school bus, your operating cash pays for it. If you don't own vehicles but rent them, you still need Hired Auto coverage. If employees use their own cars for ballot pickup, you still need Non-Owned Auto Liability. Personal auto policies categorically exclude business use; the carrier denies and the exposure lands on the company. Maricopa requires $2M CSL — there is currently $0.
findings.recommendation: Confirm a Commercial Auto policy exists. If none, place Auto immediately at $2M CSL on a Symbol 1 (Any Auto) basis — covering owned, hired, and non-owned. Add Drive Other Car / Employee as Insured (CA 9933), MCS-90 if any interstate freight is moved for hire, blanket AI/WoS/Primary-Noncontributory endorsements, and Hired/Non-Owned Auto Physical Damage. If the company genuinely owns no vehicles, a 'no-owned' Auto policy or HNOA endorsement on the GL still must be placed.
discoveryQuestions: How does a tray of ballots actually move from your facility to a county elections office — your trucks, hired carriers, employees in personal cars, or all three?
If an employee rear-ended someone tomorrow on the way to a county dropoff, whose insurance pays — yours, theirs, or both — and have you ever tested that?

Maricopa requires $2M CSL. Sacramento requires $1M. If we don't have an Auto policy, every certificate you've issued under those contracts is technically unsupported — when was the last time anyone reviewed the COIs for accuracy?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability / Errors & Omissions — Policy Entirely Missing from Program
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate. (Sacramento §II.D, §III.E) ... If professional liability coverage is written on a Claims Made form: A. The 'Retro Date' must be shown, and must be on or before the date of the Agreement ... CONTRACTOR must purchase 'extended reporting' coverage for a minimum of one (1) year after completion of the Agreement. (§V.A–C)
findings.policy_quote: No standalone Professional Liability or Errors & Omissions policy was provided. Sacramento's contract expressly bars umbrella from satisfying this requirement: 'UMBRELLA or Excess Liability policies are acceptable ... that at least follow form over the underlying insurance requirements ... (other than Professional Liability) ...' (Sacramento §II.E)
findings.gap_description: Run-Test renders election services — printing, mailing, processing, ballot handling, election mail sorting, emergency support technology — to local, county and state election officials across 31 states. This is textbook professional services exposure. The Hartford D&O policy expressly EXCLUDES claims arising from 'rendering or failure to render any services for fees' (Endorsement 19 — Manufacturing and Professional Service Exclusion, PP 00 H350 00 0616, Pg 85). Therefore the company has NO mechanism — neither standalone E&O nor entity-liability under D&O — to respond to a county claim alleging negligent ballot processing, miscount, mail handling failure, or election delivery error. Sacramento requires $1M/$1M PL on a claims-made or occurrence form with continuous retro coverage; umbrella expressly cannot fill this gap.
findings.plain_english: Election services IS professional services — and you have no policy that covers it. The Hartford D&O specifically excludes anything arising from 'rendering or failure to render services for fees,' which is your entire revenue line. If a county sues because ballots arrived late, were misprinted, or were processed incorrectly — and the suit alleges negligence in your election services — there is currently zero coverage anywhere in the program. Sacramento expressly prohibits using the umbrella to fix this gap. This is the single most existential coverage gap for your business model. A $1M E&O premium is small money compared to a county suing for damages from a botched primary.
findings.recommendation: Place standalone Election Services Professional Liability / Technology E&O immediately. Limits: minimum $1M/$1M to satisfy Sacramento; recommend $5M+ given operational scope (90M voters, 31 states). Definition of Professional Services MUST expressly include: ballot printing/design, election mail sorting and delivery, voter file processing, election technology services, ballot envelope manufacturing, signature verification support, and emergency election support. Retro date on or before the earliest active county contract. Confirm carrier offers full prior acts. Consider a combined E&O + Cyber form to also address Maricopa cyber requirement (see finding-004).
discoveryQuestions: When a county tells you ballots arrived late or were misprinted, what is your contractual exposure — and is anything in your insurance program designed to defend that allegation?

Your Hartford D&O has an exclusion that strips coverage for 'rendering or failure to render any services for fees.' That is literally what Run-Test does — has anyone walked you through what the practical effect of that exclusion is on a county dispute?
Sacramento County won't allow you to use your umbrella to satisfy the Professional Liability requirement. If a Sacramento auditor reviews your COIs tomorrow, what do we show them?
If a county election challenge alleges that your processing led to a miscount, do you know who pays the defense lawyers and who pays the settlement?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber Liability — Policy Entirely Missing from Program ($5M Required by Maricopa)
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence. The policy shall include, but not be limited to; coverage for all directors, officers, agents and employees of the Contractor, losses with respect to network risks (such as data breaches, unauthorized access or use, and ID theft of data), invasion of privacy ... crisis management, identity theft response costs, breach notification costs, credit remediation, and credit monitoring, defense, and claims expenses, regulatory defense costs plus fines and penalties, cyber extortion, electronic data restoration expenses ..., network business interruption, computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction, and loss outside the premises of the named insured.
findings.policy_quote: No standalone Cyber policy was provided. The Hartford Crime Coverage Part has narrow related coverages: Computer & Funds Transfer Fraud $2M; Deception Fraud / Social Engineering $15,000 (extremely low); and explicitly excludes 'theft or disclosure of trade secrets, intellectual property, credit card numbers, bank account numbers, etc. ... or Data (unless covered under IA 7)' per PP 00 H600 00 0616 §V(V), Pg 55. Computer Systems Restoration sublimit $25,000 only.
findings.policy_page: N/A — no Cyber policy. Hartford Crime sublimits Pg 8 (Crime Dec) and Pg 55 (exclusion).
findings.gap_description: Run-Test serves 31 states + DC, impacting 90M+ registered voters, with election technology solutions including ballot printing, mailing, processing, signature verification, and emergency support technology. This is a maximum-exposure cyber profile: large PII repositories (voter rolls), election integrity stakeholders (state AGs, DOJ, CISA), foreign-adversary threat actors, and ransomware risk. Maricopa requires $5M cyber with the broadest possible enumerated specs (regulatory FINES & PENALTIES, third-party fidelity, business interruption, cyber extortion, computer fraud, funds transfer, breach notification, credit monitoring). NO Cyber policy is in the program. The Hartford Crime form expressly excludes data/IP theft, providing only $25K computer systems restoration and $15K social engineering. Voter PII breach, ransomware on election eve, regulatory investigation by state AGs — all uninsured.
findings.plain_english: Of every coverage gap in this program, this is the one that should keep the CFO and the board up at night. Run-Test handles voter records for 90 million Americans across 31 states. Election infrastructure is on every nation-state cyber actor's target list. A ransomware attack 30 days before a primary — locking your printing systems and threatening to release voter PII — would trigger forensic costs, ransom decisions, business interruption, breach notification to 31 state AGs, regulatory defense, civil class actions, and county lawsuits for delayed mail. The current program has none of this. Hartford's Crime policy has $15,000 for social engineering and excludes data breaches. Maricopa is requiring $5M expressly. If Maricopa audits the COI today, you cannot deliver evidence of compliance — and given your industry, an auditor at the State of Arizona or any other county is going to ask. This is the immediate priority alongside Professional Liability.
findings.recommendation: Place a standalone Cyber/Tech E&O form at $5M minimum (recommend $10M given national exposure). Required coverages must include: first-party (BI/extortion/data restoration), third-party (privacy/network/regulatory defense including FINES & PENALTIES — many forms exclude or sublimit fines, get them in), social engineering at full limit (not sublimited), business interruption AND dependent business interruption, system failure trigger, bricking, voluntary parting, reputational harm, PCI assessments, election-specific endorsements where available. Retro date on or before earliest cyber-aware contract. Coordinate with E&O (finding-003) — combined Tech E&O + Cyber from a carrier specializing in election services / govtech (Coalition, At-Bay, Beazley InfoSec, Chubb Cyber Plus) is the most efficient path.
discoveryQuestions: If a ransomware actor encrypted your printing and processing systems three weeks before a primary, how would the company respond in the first 24 hours — and who pays for the response team?
You're holding voter PII for tens of millions of Americans across 31 state regulatory regimes. If even one state AG opened an investigation tomorrow, who defends it and who pays the fines?

Maricopa County requires a $5M cyber policy with regulatory FINES coverage, third-party fidelity, and cyber extortion as listed must-haves. Do we have a current certificate that satisfies that contract today?
Has anyone — internally or with us — modeled what a publicly disclosed Run-Test breach would do to your county relationships and renewal pipeline?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella / Excess Liability — Policy Entirely Missing from Program

If available, the insurance policies required by this contract may be combined with Commercial Umbrella Insurance policies to meet the minimum limit requirements. (Maricopa §8.2.9)
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §II.E Pg 2 of 4; Maricopa §8.2.9 Pg 6 of 41
findings.policy_quote: No Umbrella/Excess policy was provided in this program audit.
findings.gap_description: No Umbrella policy is present. Even if GL/Auto were placed at the $2M Maricopa underlying limits, a single bodily injury or product liability verdict in a federal/state court could exhaust primary GL aggregates within one claim. Election services, mail handling, and physical operations all carry catastrophic loss potential. Run-Test as a PE-backed company also faces enhanced regulatory and litigation exposure. The contractual indemnification obligations in Maricopa §8.1.3 are expressly NOT capped at insurance limits — uninsured tail liability falls on the balance sheet.
findings.plain_english: There's no umbrella in the program. Even when we place GL and Auto at the right limits, a single catastrophic event — a multi-vehicle delivery accident, a serious workplace injury, a product liability suit — can blow through a $2M GL aggregate in a single claim. The umbrella sits on top to absorb that. Maricopa's contract is also explicit that nothing in the insurance limits caps your indemnification obligation — meaning the County can come after Run-Test's balance sheet for any shortfall above policy limits. For a PE-backed company at this revenue scale, a $10M umbrella is table stakes; $25M is more appropriate given the geographic and operational footprint.
findings.recommendation: Place a follow-form Commercial Umbrella with minimum $10M limit (recommend $25M given 31-state operations, election scrutiny, and PE ownership). Confirm: (a) follow-form on AI, WoS, P&NC; (b) per-project / per-location aggregate follows form; (c) drop-down for exhausted underlying aggregates; (d) Defense costs OUTSIDE limits (standard market) — flag if E&S placement; (e) maintenance-of-underlying clause does NOT result in coverage forfeiture for inadvertent lapse; (f) Notice & Knowledge endorsement limited to officer/risk manager. Schedule of Underlying must list GL, Auto, EL (under WC), Foreign Voluntary if applicable. Note: Sacramento §II.E and Maricopa §8.2.9 BOTH bar Umbrella from being applied to satisfy the Professional Liability $1M minimum — Umbrella does NOT cure finding-003.
discoveryQuestions: If a delivery vehicle were involved in a multi-vehicle accident with serious injuries to multiple parties, do you know what your maximum exposure is — and what limit you'd want to defend yourself with?

Your contracts with both Sacramento and Maricopa say insurance limits do NOT cap your indemnification obligation — meaning anything above the policy comes out of the company. How comfortable is the board with that exposure today?
Have you ever had a claim or near-claim that approached or exceeded a primary GL aggregate? What did that conversation with leadership look like?

findings.requirement_type: D&O — Manufacturing and Professional Services Exclusion (Hartford)
findings.contract_quote: (D&O coverage is broadly required by lender covenants, board governance and PE sponsor expectations; not contractually required by Sacramento or Maricopa, but core balance-sheet protection.)
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #19 EXCLUSION FOR MANUFACTURING AND PROFESSIONAL SERVICE ENDORSEMENT: 'The Insurer shall not be liable for Loss on account of any Claim made against any Insured based upon, arising from, or in any way related to: (1) the malfunction of any product or product failure due to any deficiency, inadequacy, defect, or dangerous condition in such product or in its design or manufacture; or (2) the rendering of or failure to render any services for a fee, including any services rendered by an Insured for a customer or client of any Insured.' Carve-backs: securities-holder civil proceedings without Insured solicitation; Derivative Action / Derivative Demand. (PP 00 H350 00 0616)
findings.policy_page: Pg 85 — Endorsement #19, Hartford Twin City Management Liability 59 KB 0575120-24
findings.gap_description: This exclusion is the most damaging endorsement in the entire program for Run-Test's business model. Run-Test's revenue is entirely 'services for a fee' — printing, mailing, processing, election technology — to county/state customers. The exclusion bars D&O Side B (corporate reimbursement) and Side C (entity liability) coverage for any Claim arising from these core operations. The carve-backs only preserve coverage for: (a) securities-holder civil suits brought without insider solicitation; and (b) derivative actions/demands. This means: (i) a county lawsuit naming directors/officers individually for service-delivery failures = excluded; (ii) state AG investigations of corporate conduct re: election services = excluded; (iii) regulatory actions arising from product/service failures = excluded. For a PE-backed election services manufacturer, this exclusion neuters the policy's most likely-to-trigger applications. Aligns with 2026-03-24 lesson learned re: Hartford Private Choice Premier.
findings.plain_english: This is the worst endorsement in the policy for your business specifically. Hartford has carved out coverage for any claim arising from rendering services for fees or product malfunction. Your entire revenue line — every dollar — is 'services for a fee' to counties. So if a county sues your directors and officers personally because ballots were processed incorrectly, the policy will deny. The only things that are still covered are very narrow: shareholder lawsuits, and derivative actions. Functionally you have D&O coverage for Wall Street-style claims and almost nothing for the Main Street claims that would actually hit a privately held election services company. The PE sponsor should be aware of this — they probably are not.
findings.recommendation: At renewal (4/1/2026 expiry), prioritize replacing or renegotiating this exclusion. Options in order of preference: (1) Move to a carrier that does not impose this exclusion on election technology / govtech firms (e.g., AIG, Travelers Bond, Berkshire's BHSI, Chubb, Beazley) — many will quote without it; (2) Negotiate a carve-back for non-securities claims by governmental/contractual customers; (3) At minimum negotiate carve-back for non-indemnifiable Side A coverage; (4) If Hartford remains the carrier, demand the exclusion be deleted in exchange for a premium increase. Until renewal, advise the board in writing that D&O Side B/C coverage for service-delivery claims is materially limited. PE sponsor counsel should be looped in.
discoveryQuestions: If a county attorney named your CEO and CFO personally in a lawsuit alleging that Run-Test's ballot processing caused election errors, what's your understanding of how the D&O policy would respond?
Has the PE sponsor — Lincoln Shields or Black Mountain — ever asked you to confirm what is and isn't covered under your D&O for service-delivery disputes?

When was the last time your D&O policy was marketed to multiple carriers? Hartford's policy has an exclusion that strips coverage for almost every claim type your business would actually face — that's worth shopping aggressively at renewal.
If the Department of Justice or a state AG opened an investigation into your election services tomorrow, do you understand what investigation costs would and wouldn't be covered?

findings.requirement_type: Crime — IP / Confidential Information / Data Exclusion (Voter PII)
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance ... losses with respect to network risks (such as data breaches, unauthorized access or use, and ID theft of data), invasion of privacy (regardless of the type of media involved in the loss of private information) ... (Maricopa §8.2.13)
findings.policy_quote: Crime §V(V): excludes loss involving 'theft or disclosure of trade secrets, intellectual property, credit card numbers, bank account numbers, etc. (unless covered under IA 8 Identity Recovery), or Data (unless covered under IA 7).' Identity Recovery (IA 8) is restricted to personal identities of named officers/directors/risk managers/in-house counsel — NOT the business itself. Computer Systems Restoration (IA 7) sublimit $25,000.
findings.policy_page: Pg 55 — PP 00 H600 00 0616 §V(V); Pg 8 — Crime Dec sublimits
findings.gap_description: Run-Test holds voter records affecting 90M+ registered voters across 31 states. The Crime policy explicitly excludes data, IP and confidential information theft. The only data-restoration coverage is Computer Systems Restoration at $25,000 — a fraction of the cost of even a contained ransomware response. There is no first-party data privacy coverage, no breach notification coverage, no regulatory defense coverage anywhere in the program. Combined with finding-004, voter PII breach has zero meaningful coverage in the current program.
findings.plain_english: The Hartford Crime piece is what some companies use as a stand-in for cyber when they don't have a real Cyber policy. For Run-Test that doesn't work — the Crime form expressly excludes any loss tied to data, IP, or confidential information. The $25,000 of computer systems restoration wouldn't cover a single day of a real ransomware response. So even setting the Cyber gap aside (finding-004), the Crime piece doesn't quietly fill it.
findings.recommendation: Treat as part of the Cyber placement priority (finding-004). Do not rely on Crime IA 7 or IA 8 for any data-related exposure. Once Cyber is placed, ensure no double-indemnification gap between Cyber and Crime — coordinate definitions of 'Money,' 'Securities,' 'Computer Fraud,' and 'Funds Transfer Fraud' across both forms.
discoveryQuestions: If a Run-Test laptop containing voter signature images was stolen out of an employee's car, what would actually happen — who responds, who pays for notification to the affected voters?
Have you ever quantified the cost of breach notification to voters across your 31 states? Each state has different timing rules and some require credit monitoring at the carrier's cost.
Your Crime policy will not cover data loss. Did anyone explain to you that the $25,000 'Computer Systems Restoration' line is not a substitute for cyber coverage?

findings.requirement_type: Crime — Deception Fraud (Social Engineering) Sublimit Materially Inadequate
findings.contract_quote: Cyber ... computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction ... (Maricopa §8.2.13)
findings.policy_quote: Crime Coverage Part Declarations (Pg 8): Deception Fraud (Social Engineering) $15,000 limit per occurrence. Other Crime IAs (Employee Theft, Forgery, Inside/Outside Premises, Computer Fraud, Funds Transfer Fraud) all $2,000,000.
findings.policy_page: Pg 8, Crime Coverage Part Declarations, Hartford 59 KB 0575120-24
findings.gap_description: Social engineering attacks (CEO impersonation wire-transfer fraud, vendor email compromise) are the dominant theft vector for any company processing payments for counties or paying vendors at scale. The $15,000 sublimit is dramatically below industry norm ($250K-$500K standard, $1M+ for high-exposure firms). For a company with $5M-$25M revenue and county-payment workflows, a single CEO-impersonation wire of $250,000-$750,000 is plausible — and the policy will pay only $15,000 of it.
findings.plain_english: Social engineering is the modern bank heist. Someone impersonates your CEO or a county finance officer, sends an urgent wire request, and your AP team approves it. The Hartford Crime policy will pay $15,000. A single average loss is in the hundreds of thousands. That's not insurance, that's a deductible.
findings.recommendation: At renewal (4/1/2026), increase Deception Fraud / Social Engineering sublimit to a minimum of $250,000 and ideally to the full $2M Crime limit if available. If Hartford caps it at $250K-$500K, place separate Cyber form (per finding-004) with Social Engineering limit of $1M+. Implement carrier-required dual-authentication and callback-verification controls to maintain coverage; many carriers now require these as conditions precedent.
discoveryQuestions: What's your current process when someone in finance receives a wire-transfer request that looks urgent and comes from the CEO or a senior county contact?
Have any of your AP staff ever received a phishing or impersonation email that looked legitimate? How was it caught?
If a $300,000 wire went out tomorrow on a forged executive request, would the company recover it through insurance? The current sublimit is $15,000.

findings.requirement_type: D&O / EPLI / Fiduciary — Prior Acts Exclusion (1-Year Cutoff)

Any wrongful act, employment practice, fiduciary breach, or related claim arising from conduct before 8/18/2023 is uninsured under all three liability coverage parts. For a PE-backed company (per CLAUDE.md guidance to scrutinize prior acts on PE deals), this is a meaningful concern — typical PE-driven D&O placements feature continuous prior acts back to the LBO date or earlier.
findings.plain_english: Your D&O, EPL, and Fiduciary policies only cover conduct from August 2023 forward. Run-Test has been operating for 50+ years. If an employee filed an EPL suit today alleging harassment that occurred in 2022 — uncovered. If a former plan participant sues over a fiduciary decision made before the policy started — uncovered. For a PE-backed company, this is a known soft spot that PE sponsor counsel often demands be fixed at renewal or via separate run-off coverage.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, negotiate full prior acts (back to entity inception or at minimum the PE acquisition date). If carrier resists, consider purchasing tail / Side A DIC over the existing primary, or place a separate runoff policy for pre-8/18/2023 exposures. Discuss with PE sponsor representatives — they may have cross-portfolio carrier arrangements that include better prior acts.
discoveryQuestions: When the PE sponsors acquired Run-Test, was there a tail policy purchased for pre-acquisition wrongful acts? If not, what coverage protects pre-acquisition conduct today?
If a former employee sued for retaliation alleging conduct from 2022, what's your understanding of how the EPL responds?
Has the PE sponsor's General Counsel reviewed your prior acts coverage on D&O? Most PE shops require continuous prior acts.

findings.requirement_type: D&O — Split Prior or Pending Date on Upper $1M Layer
findings.contract_quote: (Internal governance / placement integrity)
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #34 — Amended Declarations Split Prior or Pending Date: '04/02/2024 ... applies ONLY to the additional/increased $1,000,000 layer in excess of the first $1,000,000.' (PP 00 H105 00 0616)
findings.gap_description: First $1M D&O has older Prior or Pending date; upper $1M layer (in excess) has 4/2/2024 P&P date. Any matter pending or threatened between 8/18/2023 and 4/2/2024 is excluded from the upper $1M but covered under the first $1M — creating a 'donut' where catastrophic claims exceeding $1M find no excess support if rooted in matters pending during that window.
findings.plain_english: Your first $1M of D&O has one effective date for prior matters; the second $1M (which only kicks in when the first is exhausted) has a different, later effective date. So if a board-level dispute or lawsuit was simmering in late 2023 to early 2024 and breaks today and exceeds $1M, the upper layer denies — even though the first $1M would respond. Most placements don't do this; it's a renewal-time fix.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, request the upper $1M layer's Prior or Pending date be aligned with the first $1M's date (or eliminated entirely). If the carrier refuses, consider replacing the upper $1M with a different excess carrier that will provide aligned P&P.
discoveryQuestions: Are you aware of any board, employment, or fiduciary matter that was unresolved between August 2023 and April 2024 — even informally?
If a $1.5M D&O claim broke today and was rooted in something pending in late 2023, do you understand how only half of it would be covered?

For all other county clients across the 31 states, build a master schedule and endorse all required counties onto every policy's designated-entity NOC at next renewal.

If your WC policy were canceled tomorrow, how would Maricopa learn — and would they consider the contract in breach if the notice came late?

findings.contract_quote: (Best practice — supports 31-state operations)

findings.requirement_type: WC — Favorable Experience Modifier
findings.contract_quote: (Premium efficiency / safety-program quality indicator)
findings.policy_quote: Experience Modifier: AZ 0.69, AR 0.66, CO 0.69, FL 0.69, GA 0.69, IL 0.69, IN 0.69, MN 0.69, NC 0.69, OR 0.69, SD 0.69, NY 0.97, PA 0.95 (merit credit). California Schedule Modification 0.52, Arizona Schedule Modification 0.75.
findings.gap_description: Mod factors well below 1.0 across all NCCI states reflect a strong safety record relative to industry peers — translating to ~31% premium credit nationally and a 48% schedule mod credit in California. This is a meaningful indicator of effective safety programs.
findings.plain_english: Your experience modifier — the multiplier the carrier uses to scale your WC premium based on past loss experience — is 0.69 in most states, meaning you're paying about 31% less than an average employer for the same operations. California's 0.52 schedule modification is even better. This reflects a safety program working well; it also makes you a significantly better insured to market on renewal.
findings.recommendation: Maintain return-to-work and safety programs. At each renewal, request a side-by-side review of small indemnity claims to identify any that could be re-treated as medical-only (some NCCI states permit a 70% reduction for mod calculation purposes). If revenue grows, consider negotiating composite rating. Strong mod is leverage at WC renewal — use it.

findings.policy_page: Schedule of Operations not detailed in analysis
findings.gap_description: WC class codes drive both premium and (occasionally) coverage scope. Election services / ballot printing / mail processing / signature verification are non-standard operations that may be variously classed as: 4304 Newspaper Publishing, 8742 Salespersons-Outside, 8810 Clerical, 8742 Outside Sales, 9079 Restaurant (no), 8868 College/Schools (no), 8017 Stores Retail, or potentially 4279 Paper Goods Mfg / 8810/8825 Clerical. Election services is unusual enough that the codes are easy to get wrong, and class-code mismatches show up at audit as a premium adjustment — sometimes meaningful. This is a verification step, not a finding of error.
findings.recommendation: Request the Schedule of Operations / classification breakout from Hanover. Walk every code line-by-line against actual job duties (printing, mail processing, software development, sales, clerical, outside service, drivers). Identify any miscoding before the audit. If any code is in dispute, file an NCCI inspection request.

findings.requirement_type: WC — Notice & Knowledge Endorsement (Officer-Limited)
findings.contract_quote: (RMF Gen-4 — always-emit item)
findings.policy_quote: No 'Notice Manager' or 'Knowledge of Occurrence' or 'Imputation of Knowledge' endorsement was identified in the WC endorsement schedule. Standard WC 00 00 00 C imputes knowledge broadly.
findings.gap_description: Standard WC policy treats notice/knowledge of an occurrence as triggered by any insured. Best practice is to endorse policies so that notice triggers only when officer/risk manager/insurance contact is notified — preventing low-level employee knowledge from being imputed to the entity. WC carriers often resist this because WC operates differently from liability lines. This is a verification item — confirm whether such endorsement exists.
findings.plain_english: On the management liability policy, the carrier has limited 'notice' to your CEO and CFO — meaning a lower-level employee learning of something doesn't automatically trigger reporting obligations. We want the same treatment on the workers' comp side. We don't see evidence of it in the policy. Worth confirming with Hanover.
findings.recommendation: Confirm with Hanover whether a Notice Manager / Imputation of Knowledge endorsement is available for the WC policy. WC carriers often will not amend this on standard NCCI forms, but worth asking. Implement an internal incident-reporting protocol so that incidents reach the Risk Manager promptly regardless.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Hartford Management Liability — Notice Manager limited to CEO/CFO via Endt #10 (PP 00 H022 00 0616, Pg 74)

findings.requirement_type: WC — Alternate Employer Endorsement (If Using Staffing/Leased Workers)
findings.contract_quote: (RMF WC-5 — Alternate Employer Endorsement on leasing company's policy)
findings.policy_quote: No Alternate Employer Endorsement identified on the Hanover WC policy. If Run-Test uses temporary staffing for ballot processing peaks, the staffing agency's policy should carry an Alternate Employer endorsement naming Run-Test.
findings.gap_description: Election services are seasonal — significant staffing surges around primaries and general elections. If Run-Test uses temp/staffing agencies, those agencies' WC policies should include an Alternate Employer Endorsement naming Run-Test as an alternate employer. Without it, if a staffing-agency worker is injured at Run-Test's facility, the staffing agency's WC may pay benefits but Run-Test could face EL or third-party-over actions.
findings.plain_english: Election services is seasonal — you almost certainly bring in temps around primaries and general elections. When you do, the staffing agency's workers' comp should name Run-Test as an 'alternate employer.' Without that, if a temp gets hurt at your facility, you're exposed to legal action even though they're not technically your employee. We'd want to confirm what staffing arrangements are in place and whether the necessary endorsements are on those staffing-agency policies.
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether Run-Test uses staffing agencies or PEOs for seasonal labor. If yes: (a) request COIs from each staffing partner showing Alternate Employer Endorsement naming Run-Test; (b) require this in vendor contracts going forward; (c) consider adding 'Leased Workers excluded as Employees' language on the GL once placed; (d) request the Lessor add the alternate employer endorsement to their WC.

findings.requirement_type: Named Insured Asymmetry — Inc vs LLC Across Program
findings.contract_quote: (RMF Gen-3 — Named insureds for each policy and flag any missing)
findings.policy_quote: Hanover WC Named Insured: 'Runbeck Election Services Inc' (Inc). Additional Named Insureds: 'Investments LLC,' 'Properties LLC,' 'Graphics Inc' (entity names partially redacted). Hartford Management Liability Named Insured: 'Runbeck Election Services, LLC' (LLC). No additional named insureds listed on Hartford ML.
findings.policy_file: redacted - Hanover - WC - 4.1.25-4.1.26.pdf / Redacted2024-26 Management Liability Policy.pdf
findings.gap_description: The Named Insured on the WC policy is 'Runbeck Election Services Inc' while the Named Insured on the Management Liability policy is 'Runbeck Election Services, LLC.' These are two different entity types. Either: (1) one is a legacy / typo'd designation that does not match the actual entity (in which case coverage may be void as 'not in the name of the insured'); or (2) there are two separate entities (Inc and LLC) and they are not consistently named across the program. The Hartford ML also has no additional named insureds — the related LLCs (Investments LLC, Properties LLC) and the Graphics Inc that ARE on the WC are NOT on the ML, which means D&O/EPLI/Fiduciary/Crime do not extend to those entities at all unless they qualify as Subsidiaries under the policy's automatic-acquisition definition.
findings.plain_english: Your two policies don't agree on what kind of entity Run-Test is. The workers' comp says 'Inc.' The management liability says 'LLC.' One of them is wrong, or there are two entities with similar names. Either way it's a real problem — carriers occasionally deny claims when the entity name on the policy doesn't precisely match the entity that suffered the loss. Beyond that, the WC policy lists three related companies (an investments LLC, a properties LLC, and a graphics Inc), but the management liability policy doesn't list any of them — so D&O, EPL, Fiduciary, and Crime coverage doesn't extend to those affiliates.
findings.recommendation: (1) Confirm with the client the legal entity structure — is the operating company an Inc or an LLC, and what are the related affiliates? (2) Reconcile Named Insureds across every policy in the program. (3) Add the affiliated LLCs and Graphics Inc to the Hartford Management Liability either as additional named insureds or confirm they fall within the Subsidiary definition (PP 00 H113 00 0517 extends to controlled 501(c)(3)s but standard subsidiary requires >50% ownership). (4) When GL/Auto/Umbrella/Cyber are placed, ensure consistent named-insured schedule across all policies.
discoveryQuestions: Walk me through the corporate structure — is the operating entity an Inc or an LLC, and what are the related companies (the investments, properties, and graphics entities on the WC)?
If a director-level claim or employment lawsuit hit one of the related LLCs, what's your understanding of how the Hartford management liability policy responds to it?
Has the PE sponsor's counsel reviewed your insurance program's named-insured schedule against the actual ownership chart?

findings.requirement_type: Carrier A.M. Best Rating — Verification Required
findings.contract_quote: Insurance is to be placed with insurers with a current A.M. Best's rating of no less than A-VII. (Sacramento §VI.A.1) ... an AM Best, Inc. category rating of B++. (Maricopa §8.2.1)
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §VI.A.1 Pg 3 of 4; Maricopa §8.2.1 Pg 5 of 41
findings.policy_quote: Hanover WC carrier: 'Massachusetts Bay Insurance Company (Hanover Insurance Group).' Hartford ML carrier: 'Twin City Fire Insurance Co. (a Hartford company).' Per-policy analysis JSONs do not include current A.M. Best ratings.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento requires A-VII or better (typically Hanover Mass Bay carries A or A+ rating with size category VIII-IX, Twin City carries A+ with very large size category). Maricopa requires B++ minimum (a much lower threshold both carriers easily satisfy). Need to confirm current Best ratings as of policy effective dates, and especially as new policies (GL/Auto/Umbrella/Cyber/E&O) are placed — the additional policies must each independently meet A-VII for Sacramento.
findings.plain_english: Both contracts require carriers at or above an A.M. Best minimum rating. Maricopa allows B++ (low). Sacramento requires A-VII (much higher). Both Hanover and Hartford historically meet A-VII with room to spare, but ratings should be confirmed as of the policy effective date. More important: as we place GL, Auto, Umbrella, Cyber, and E&O, every one of those carriers will need to meet A-VII independently — that's the gating criterion for any Sacramento-related placement.
findings.recommendation: Pull current A.M. Best reports on Massachusetts Bay Insurance Company and Twin City Fire Insurance Company — file in client folder. As each new policy (GL/Auto/PL/Cyber/Umbrella) is placed for findings 1-5, confirm the carrier meets A-VII before binding. Document carrier ratings on every COI issued to Sacramento and Maricopa.

findings.requirement_type: Cancellation / Material Change Notice — Hartford Management Liability AZ Form
findings.contract_quote: Applicable to all insurance policies required ... Contractor's insurance shall not be permitted to expire, be suspended, be canceled, or be materially changed for any reason without 30 days prior written notice to Maricopa County. (Maricopa §8.2.15)
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #32 (HR 02 H003 01 — AZ Cancellation and Nonrenewal): 'Insurer may ONLY cancel for nonpayment — 10 days written notice by certified mail. Nonrenewal: 45 days written notice by certified mail.'
findings.gap_description: The Hartford ML policy provides 10 days carrier-issued cancellation notice for non-payment in AZ (per state mandate) — shorter than Maricopa's 30-day requirement to County. The contractor must therefore relay any received cancellation notice within 2 business days. The carrier itself does not provide direct designated-entity notice to Maricopa (no NOC endorsement on Hartford ML).
findings.plain_english: The management liability policy can be canceled by Hartford with as little as 10 days notice for non-payment. Your Maricopa contract requires 30 days notice to the County. The fix is your contract obliges YOU to relay any cancellation notice to Maricopa within two business days — but it's worth ensuring AP knows that and the workflow is documented.
findings.recommendation: (1) Add Maricopa County (and Sacramento County, El Paso, Coconino, Amazon, and any other contractually required entity) to a master 'designated entity' list and request designated-entity NOC endorsements on every policy where carrier offers them. (2) Document an internal protocol: any cancellation/non-renewal notice received from any carrier triggers a 2-business-day relay to all designated entities. (3) Prefer EFT/auto-pay on premium to eliminate non-payment cancellation risk.
discoveryQuestions: If Hartford issued a non-payment cancellation notice tomorrow, who in finance/AP would see it first and what's the protocol for getting it to the counties within two business days?
Are all the management liability premiums on auto-pay/EFT to eliminate the risk of accidental non-payment cancellation?

findings.requirement_type: EPLI — Wage & Hour Defense $100K Sublimit
findings.contract_quote: (RMF CGL-15 — EPLI Wage and Hour defense)
findings.policy_quote: EPLI Wage & Hour Defense Sublimit: $100,000. Coverage form excludes 'Wage & Hour Violations' substantively, with a defense-cost-only carve-back capped at the sublimit (sublimit erodes EPLI aggregate).
findings.gap_description: Run-Test has a hourly-paid printing/mailing/processing workforce — a textbook wage-and-hour class action target (off-the-clock claims, meal/rest break violations in CA, donning/doffing time, misclassification). Defense costs alone for a single wage-and-hour class action routinely exceed $500K-$1M; the $100K sublimit is exhausted on motions practice. No indemnity coverage for the underlying wage claim itself.
findings.plain_english: Wage and hour class actions are the most common employment claim against a business with hourly production employees. A single class action defending off-the-clock allegations across your printing and mailing operations would burn $100,000 in legal fees in the first month — and that's all you have. After that, defense and any settlement come out of company cash. California operations make this exposure higher because CA wage-and-hour law is the most aggressive in the country.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, request increase to at least $250,000 - $500,000 wage-and-hour defense sublimit. Some carriers will also offer dedicated Wage & Hour standalone coverage (Beazley, Argo, Hiscox) — recommend evaluating. Implement payroll/timekeeping controls (audit off-the-clock time, meal/rest break compliance esp. in CA, classification of any salaried-exempt election services staff) to reduce frequency.
discoveryQuestions: How many hourly employees does Run-Test have, and how is timekeeping handled — paper, badge, app, supervisor-tracked?
Have you ever had a wage-and-hour DOL inquiry, an off-the-clock allegation, or an employee complaint about meal/rest breaks — especially from California operations?
If a class-action wage suit was filed tomorrow, your EPLI would pay $100,000 toward defense before going dry. What's the next dollar — operating cash or another policy?

findings.requirement_type: EPLI — Workplace Violence Coverage (Expense-Only, No Third-Party Liability)
findings.contract_quote: (Operational risk evaluation)
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #31 — Workplace Violence Coverage: '$100K sublimit per Dec. Pays BI Expenses up to 90 days, Employee salary/wages up to 90 days, counseling, security guard up to 30 days, security consultant, PR firm. NO Retention. EXCLUDES war/insurrection/riot AND extortion-driven force AND legal costs/attorneys' fees/settlements/judgments — EXPENSE-only coverage, NOT third-party liability.'
findings.gap_description: Workplace Violence coverage is expense reimbursement only — counseling, security, PR. It does NOT cover legal costs, settlements, or judgments from third-party suits filed by injured employees, families of deceased, or visitors. Election workplaces have heightened threat profile (politically motivated actors). A workplace shooting incident's litigation costs would flow to GL (premises liability), Umbrella (when placed), and EPLI third-party coverage — none of which are confirmed adequate or in place.
findings.plain_english: If there were a workplace violence incident, the policy will reimburse the company for crisis response — security, counseling, PR — up to $100,000. But if the families of injured or deceased employees later sue the company for inadequate security, the workplace violence endorsement explicitly DOES NOT pay defense or settlement. That part flows to GL (which we don't have on file — see finding-001) and EPLI third-party coverage. Election services has a heightened threat profile. Worth raising the limit and tightening the surrounding coverage.
findings.recommendation: (1) Once GL and Umbrella are placed (findings 1, 5), confirm premises liability covers third-party physical-injury claims arising from workplace violence. (2) At ML renewal, request increase to $250K-$500K WPV expense limit given threat profile. (3) Consider Active Assailant standalone coverage (Beazley, AIG, McGowan) which typically offers third-party liability AND expense in a single product. (4) Implement / audit physical security plan — many carriers now require documented WPV plans as a condition of coverage.
discoveryQuestions: Election services workers and facilities have been targeted in recent years. What does your physical security look like at production sites, and have you done a threat assessment?
If there were a workplace violence incident at a Run-Test facility, the families of the affected would likely sue alleging inadequate security. Do you understand how that lawsuit gets defended today?
Have you considered an Active Assailant standalone policy? They package the crisis response, third-party liability, and business interruption together.

findings.requirement_type: D&O — Personal Asset Protection / Co-Defendants Extension (PE-Specific)
findings.contract_quote: (Internal governance / PE sponsor protection)
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #7 (PP 00 M119 00 0120): 'Damages now includes Personal Asset Protection Costs incurred by President/CEO/CFO of Named Entity to oppose enforcement-authority efforts to seize personal assets/real estate.' Endorsement #33 (PP 00 H050 00 0616 Co-Defendants Extension): 'PE-SPECIFIC. Named Co-Defendants: Lincoln Shields, LLC and Black Mountain Investment Company, LLC. Defines Affiliated Entities ... and Co-Defendants. Coverage requires (i) actual/alleged Wrongful Act of an Insured, (ii) Claim first against Insured, (iii) Co-Defendants joined by reason of ownership/management control of Named Entity, (iv) same counsel.' Endorsement #9 (PP 00 H125 00 0718): 'Manager now includes de facto or shadow directors.'
findings.gap_description: These endorsements collectively address PE-specific risks identified in CLAUDE.md: (1) Lincoln Shields and Black Mountain (the PE sponsors) are named as Co-Defendants and receive coverage when joined to a claim against the company; (2) shadow-director status protects PE sponsor representatives who may not hold formal director seats; (3) personal asset protection extends to enforcement-authority actions against CEO/CFO/President.
findings.plain_english: The Hartford policy was specifically tailored for the PE sponsor structure. Lincoln Shields and Black Mountain are named as Co-Defendants — meaning when they get pulled into a lawsuit because they own Run-Test, the policy responds as long as the suit is rooted in something the company allegedly did. Shadow-director protection covers PE-side representatives who don't formally sit on the board but exercise control. And personal asset protection covers the executive team if a regulator tries to freeze personal assets. These are good things — credit where it's due.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal. Verify Lincoln Shields LLC and Black Mountain Investment Company LLC remain the correct sponsor entities (no fund vintage change, no SPV restructure). Confirm any new fund vehicle or co-investor is added at the time the change occurs. Coordinate with PE sponsor's portfolio insurance program to ensure no double-coverage gaps on Run-Test board members.

findings.requirement_type: D&O — Side A Additional Limit for Managers ($1M)
findings.contract_quote: (Internal governance — Side A protection)
findings.policy_quote: Additional Limit for Managers (Insuring Agreement A): $1,000,000. Sits over and above the $2M D&O Aggregate, accessible only for non-indemnifiable Insured Person Loss.
findings.gap_description: $1M dedicated Side A in addition to the $2M D&O aggregate. Provides last-dollar protection for individual directors/officers when entity indemnification is unavailable (insolvency, derivative actions where indemnification barred, regulatory action). For PE-backed companies this is a meaningful added layer.
findings.plain_english: Beyond the main $2M D&O limit, there's an additional $1M reserved exclusively for individual directors and officers — accessible only when the company can't legally indemnify them (the most dangerous scenario for an executive personally). This is an important Side A layer.
findings.recommendation: Maintain. At renewal consider whether to add a separate Side A DIC (difference-in-conditions) tower over the entire D&O — common for PE-backed companies preparing for IPO or where personal indemnification certainty matters.

findings.requirement_type: Crime — Employee Theft & Computer Fraud at $2M
findings.contract_quote: (Maricopa cyber spec also requires 'computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity' — partial overlap with Crime, primary coverage to come from Cyber per finding-004)
findings.policy_quote: Crime Coverage Part Declarations: Employee Theft $2M; Forgery or Alteration $2M; Inside Premises $2M; Outside Premises $2M; Computer & Funds Transfer Fraud $2M.
findings.gap_description: Core Crime sublimits at $2M each are adequate for a $5M-$25M revenue PE-backed company. Computer & Funds Transfer Fraud at $2M provides meaningful protection against system-based theft (separate from social engineering / Deception Fraud which is materially under-limited per finding-008).
findings.plain_english: Most of the Crime policy is properly limited — employee theft, forgery, computer fraud, and funds transfer fraud are all at $2M, which is appropriate for the company size. The exception is the social engineering piece at $15,000 (see finding-008). The core fidelity coverage is solid.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal. Confirm Computer Fraud and Funds Transfer Fraud language in the form aligns with the Cyber form's parallel coverages once Cyber is placed (finding-004) — coordinate definitions to avoid double-recovery disputes between carriers.

findings.requirement_type: Fiduciary — $1M Limit / COBRA $1M Sublimit / HIPAA $500K
findings.contract_quote: (ERISA / employee benefits compliance)
findings.policy_quote: Fiduciary Aggregate $1M, $0 retention. COBRA Claim Sublimit $1M (Endt #18, PP 00 M073 00 0719). HIPAA Sublimit $500K. ERISA §502(c) Penalty Sublimit $50K. PPA / UK Pensions / ACA Penalty Sublimit $250K.
findings.gap_description: Fiduciary $1M with $0 retention is favorable structure. COBRA at $1M sublimit is robust (notable given recent COBRA notice litigation trend). HIPAA $500K and ERISA §502(c) $50K are within market norms but could be increased given a 50-200 employee workforce.
findings.plain_english: Employee benefits liability — the duty to act prudently with the 401(k) plan, the obligation to send proper COBRA notices, HIPAA privacy on health benefits — is properly addressed. $1M is a reasonable limit for a company of Run-Test's size. The COBRA notice sublimit at $1M is a notable upgrade given a recent litigation trend in COBRA claims. There's no retention, which is also favorable.
findings.recommendation: Maintain. At renewal, monitor whether plan asset growth (or any new ESOP feature, deferred-comp, NQDC) warrants increasing aggregate to $2M. If a 401(k) plan exceeds $50M in plan assets, consider increasing limits.

findings.requirement_type: Property / Inland Marine — Policies Not in Audit Submission (Election Equipment)

Any Inland Marine insurance policies maintained by the CONTRACTOR ... shall be endorsed to state that the insurer shall waive all rights of subrogation against the COUNTY. (Sacramento §IX)
findings.policy_quote: No Property or Inland Marine policy provided in this audit submission.
