Property and Inland Marine policies are almost certainly in place but were not provided for this audit. Sacramento's contract conditionally requires Loss Payee designation on any COC policy and Waiver of Subrogation on any Inland Marine policy. Without seeing the policies, we cannot confirm compliance.
findings.plain_english: We don't have your Property or Inland Marine policies in front of us. Given the high-value equipment, ballot inventory, and election technology you operate, you almost certainly have these. Sacramento's contract has specific requirements: any course-of-construction policy needs the County as loss payee, and any Inland Marine needs to waive subrogation against the County. findings.requirement_type: Cross-Program — Unintentional Errors & Omissions Giveback
findings.contract_quote: (RMF Gen-2 — always-emit item)
findings.policy_quote: No Unintentional Errors and Omissions giveback endorsement identified on Hanover WC. Hartford ML is a different policy type (not GL-based). Cannot evaluate on GL/Auto/Cyber/Umbrella because those policies are not in the program (findings 1-5).
findings.gap_description: The Unintentional E&O giveback addresses inadvertent failure to report a location/vehicle/operation. Without it, a missed location/vehicle on the schedule may be denied at claim time. This is most often an issue on GL and Property forms (rather than WC). Cannot fully evaluate because GL/Auto/Property are not in the audit submission.
findings.plain_english: Most companies with multiple locations or vehicles benefit from a small endorsement that says: 'if we accidentally forgot to tell you about a new site or vehicle, you'll still cover it as long as we report it when we find out.' Without it, an oversight at the time you opened a new facility could mean uninsured exposure there. We can't evaluate this until we have the GL and Auto policies.

findings.requirement_type: Subcontractor Pass-Through / Flow-Down Insurance Requirements
findings.contract_quote: SUBCONTRACTORS: CONTRACTOR shall be responsible for the acts and omissions of all its subcontractors and additional insured endorsements as provided by CONTRACTOR's subcontractor. (Sacramento §VII.E)
findings.policy_quote: (Subcontractor flow-down is a contractual obligation on Run-Test, not a policy provision.)
findings.gap_description: Sacramento makes Run-Test responsible for subcontractor acts/omissions and for ensuring subs provide AI endorsements. This implies a flow-down obligation: Run-Test must contractually impose matching insurance requirements on its subs (USPS contractors, mail consolidators, IT vendors, software developers, equipment suppliers). Need to verify Run-Test has standardized subcontractor agreements with insurance schedules that mirror or exceed the upstream county requirements.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento makes you legally responsible for whatever your subcontractors do or fail to do. So when you hire a mail-handling vendor or a software developer, your contract with them needs to require they carry matching insurance and name Sacramento as additional insured on their policies — and you need to collect their COIs. This is a process question, not a policy gap.
findings.recommendation: (1) Audit subcontractor insurance protocols — request the standard subcontractor agreement template. (2) Build a subcontractor insurance schedule template that flows down county insurance requirements (limits, AI, WoS, P&NC, NOC). (3) Implement COI tracking software to maintain current subcontractor COIs. (4) For high-risk subs (software developers handling voter data, mail consolidators), require Run-Test be named on their Cyber and E&O.

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento — Contractual Notification of Claim/Lawsuit (30/10 Days)
findings.contract_quote: If any claim for damages is filed with CONTRACTOR or if any lawsuit is instituted against CONTRACTOR, that arise out of or are in any way connected with CONTRACTOR's performance under this Agreement ... CONTRACTOR shall give prompt and timely notice thereof to COUNTY. Notice shall be prompt and timely if given within thirty (30) days following the date of receipt of a claim or ten (10) days following the date of service of process of a lawsuit. (Sacramento §X)
findings.policy_quote: (Contractual notification — independent of carrier notice obligations.)
findings.gap_description: This is a contractor-side process obligation, not a policy provision — but worth flagging because failure to notify Sacramento within 30/10 days = breach. Run-Test must have an internal process to identify claims/suits 'connected with CONTRACTOR's performance' and notify Sacramento promptly.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento requires you to tell them within 30 days when a claim arrives, and within 10 days when a lawsuit is served, if it touches on your contract performance. This is a workflow item — make sure your legal/risk team has a flag for any claim that comes in mentioning Sacramento or election services and the 30/10-day clock.
findings.recommendation: Build internal claims-intake protocol that flags any claim/suit referencing Sacramento performance, election services, or any of the 31 county clients. Notify county within contractual deadlines. Document notification for evidence.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa — Deductible/SIR Allocation & Bond/LOC Backing
findings.contract_quote: The insurance policies may provide coverage that contains deductibles or self-insured retentions. Such deductible and/or self-insured retentions shall not be applicable with respect to the coverage provided to County under such policies. Contractor shall be solely responsible for the deductible and/or self-insured retention and County, at its option, may require Contractor to secure payment of such deductibles or self-insured retentions by a surety bond or an irrevocable and unconditional letter of credit. (Maricopa §8.2.6)
findings.policy_quote: Hartford ML retentions: D&O $10K; EPLI $10K; Fiduciary $0; Crime variable. Hanover WC: no policy-level deductible (standard NCCI). Other policies (GL/Auto/Cyber/Umbrella) not in program.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa reserves the right to require bond or LOC backing for deductibles/SIRs. Material if SIRs exist on Cyber/E&O once placed (typical Cyber SIRs run $25K-$250K; E&O can run $25K-$100K). Bond/LOC requirements add collateral cost. Maricopa also requires the deductible/SIR not apply to the County's coverage — meaning the carrier must drop down on the AI for Maricopa's piece, or Run-Test must pay the SIR before coverage attaches.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa says: any deductibles or self-insured retentions are your problem, not theirs — and they reserve the right to make you post a bond or letter of credit to secure payment of those amounts. When we place Cyber and E&O — both of which typically have meaningful SIRs — we need to either (a) negotiate them down, (b) confirm they don't apply to Maricopa's portion of any claim, or (c) be prepared for a possible LOC requirement from the County.
findings.recommendation: (1) When new policies are placed (per findings 1-5), document all deductibles/SIRs on a single schedule. (2) Disclose to Maricopa per §8.2.6 — pre-emptively, before audit. (3) Where possible, structure Cyber/E&O with deductible-payment-by-insurer-on-AI's-behalf endorsements (some carriers offer this). (4) Maintain LOC capacity at the bank in case Maricopa invokes the bond/LOC right.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa — Indemnification Not Limited by Insurance
findings.contract_quote: The amount and type of insurance coverage requirements set forth herein will in no way be construed as limiting the scope of the indemnity in this section. (Maricopa §8.1.3) ... To the fullest extent permitted by law, and to the extent that claims, damages, losses, or expenses are not covered and paid by insurance purchased by the contractor, the contractor shall defend, indemnify, and hold harmless the County (as Owner) ... but only to the extent caused by the negligent acts or omissions of the contractor ... (Maricopa §8.1.1)
findings.policy_quote: (Contractual obligation — uncapped by insurance limits.)
findings.gap_description: Maricopa's indemnification obligation is comparative-negligence based (limited to extent of contractor fault, with sole-negligence carve-out for County) but is expressly NOT capped at insurance limits. Any indemnified amount above the (currently absent) GL/Auto/Cyber/Umbrella limits = balance-sheet exposure. Without underlying insurance in place (findings 1-5), Run-Test bears 100% of indemnified amounts directly until those policies are placed.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa's indemnification language explicitly says insurance limits do NOT cap your obligation. So even after we place GL, Auto, Cyber, and Umbrella, anything above those limits comes out of company cash. The right way to manage this is (a) place adequate primary limits, (b) place a meaningful umbrella ($10M-$25M), and (c) recognize that contractual indemnification is a tail risk that no policy fully eliminates. Right now, with most policies missing from the program, virtually every dollar of indemnification flows to the balance sheet.
findings.recommendation: (1) Place underlying GL/Auto/Cyber/Umbrella per findings 1-5 — that converts most indemnification exposure from cash to insurance. (2) Discuss with Run-Test legal counsel whether to negotiate a contractual indemnification cap with Maricopa (often resisted by counties but worth raising). (3) Maintain separate balance-sheet reserves for tail indemnification exposure not absorbed by policies. (4) Confirm with PE sponsor counsel whether parent guarantees flow up — this can affect overall corporate risk position.
discoveryQuestions: Has the company's CFO or General Counsel ever modeled the maximum exposure under the Maricopa indemnification clause for a major incident?
When you negotiate insurance limits, are you working from the assumption that limits cap exposure? Maricopa explicitly says they don't — does that change the analysis?
Has the PE sponsor reviewed the indemnification language in your county contracts and confirmed comfort with uncapped exposure?

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento — Right to Adjust Coverage Mid-Term
findings.contract_quote: COUNTY shall retain the right at any time to review the coverage, form, and amount of the insurance required hereby. If in the opinion of the County Risk Manager, insurance provisions in these requirements do not provide adequate protection ..., COUNTY may require CONTRACTOR to obtain insurance sufficient in coverage, form and amount to provide adequate protection. (Sacramento §II.B)
findings.policy_quote: (Contractual right of County, no policy provision.)
findings.gap_description: Sacramento's Risk Manager can demand additional coverage mid-term. Possible triggers include: a high-profile election incident anywhere in the country, a Run-Test loss, a county-wide procurement policy change. Open-ended risk; mid-term placement constraints possible.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento can come back at any time during the contract and tell you to buy more insurance. They typically only do this if something material has changed — your loss history, your operations, an industry incident — but the right is unilateral. Worth being aware of.
findings.recommendation: Maintain regular dialogue with Sacramento's Risk Manager. At each contract renewal cycle, proactively confirm coverage levels are acceptable. If Sacramento ever invokes this right, treat as urgent and engage with broker immediately to evaluate.

findings.requirement_type: Hartford ML — Single Retention for Multi-Coverage Claims
findings.contract_quote: (Best practice — multi-coverage claim economics)
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #29 (PP 00 H109 00 0517 — Single Retention): 'When a Claim triggers multiple Coverage Parts, only the HIGHEST applicable Retention applies — no stacking.'
findings.gap_description: When a single Claim triggers multiple coverage parts (e.g., shareholder action implicating both D&O and Fiduciary; or Whistleblower implicating D&O and EPLI), only the highest single retention applies. This avoids stacking retentions across multiple parts.
findings.plain_english: When a single legal claim hits multiple coverages — say, a board-level whistleblower suit that triggers D&O and EPL together — you only pay one retention, not two stacked. Favorable structure.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal.

findings.requirement_type: Hartford ML — Inquiry Costs Extension ($50K)
findings.contract_quote: (Regulatory investigation cost coverage)
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #3 (PP 00 M190 00 0222): '$50,000 sublimit aggregate, part of (not in addition to) Combined Aggregate Limit. Pays Inquiry Costs (written request to interview/depose Insured Person or produce documents). Applies to D&O, EPL, and Fiduciary.'
findings.gap_description: Pays for response costs to written investigative inquiries (deposition, interview, document request) — pre-Claim coverage. Useful at the early-investigation stage before a formal Claim is asserted.
findings.plain_english: If a regulator or investigator sends Run-Test a letter asking to interview an officer or produce documents — even before any formal lawsuit — the policy will pay up to $50,000 toward the cost of responding. Useful early-warning coverage. The sublimit erodes the main aggregate, so if used heavily, less remains for the eventual Claim.
findings.recommendation: Maintain. At renewal, given Run-Test's regulatory exposure (election services often draw state AG attention, DOJ Election Integrity, etc.), evaluate whether to increase to $100K-$250K. Some carriers offer this as a true 'in-addition-to' rather than 'part-of-aggregate.'

findings.requirement_type: Hartford ML — D&O Antitrust Sublimit ($1M Cap)
findings.contract_quote: (Internal governance — entity antitrust exposure)
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #16 (PP 00 H377 00 0120 — Antitrust/Unfair Trade Exclusion Sublimit): 'Antitrust/Sherman/Clayton/FTC violations subject to sublimit of lesser of remaining limit or $1,000,000.'
findings.gap_description: Antitrust claims sublimited to $1M. Better than full exclusion (which is the default for many D&O forms) but capped. For a PE-backed company in a concentrated industry (election services has limited number of national vendors), antitrust risk exists — competitor or contractor consolidation theories, exclusive-dealing claims, monopolization allegations.
findings.plain_english: If a competitor sued Run-Test for antitrust — say, alleging exclusive contracts with counties create unfair barriers to entry — the policy pays up to $1M, then stops. Antitrust litigation often runs $5M+ in defense alone. Better than full exclusion (which is what many policies have) but materially capped.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, attempt to negotiate the $1M sublimit upward (target full $2M D&O limit) or remove the carve-back. Document any competitor disputes or pricing structures that could plausibly trigger antitrust theories — gives carrier ammunition for limit increase.
discoveryQuestions: How concentrated is the election services market — how many companies could plausibly bid against Run-Test on a county RFP?
Have any counties or competitors ever raised exclusive-dealing or pricing concerns about Run-Test's contracts?
Are there county-level long-term exclusive arrangements that could be characterized as anticompetitive?

findings.requirement_type: Hartford ML — Books and Records Costs Coverage ($500K)
findings.contract_quote: (PE-backed entity — Delaware Section 220 / shareholder records demand exposure)
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #1 (PP 00 M138 00 0421): 'Adds D&O Insuring Agreement (D) Derivative Demands coverage for Books and Records Costs (e.g., Delaware Section 220 demand). $500,000 sublimit, part of (not in addition to) Investigation Costs sublimit.'
findings.gap_description: Provides coverage for response to Section 220 / books-and-records demands — a precursor to derivative litigation. PE-backed companies see these especially in transition periods (around exit, recapitalization, fund cycle changes).
findings.plain_english: Before a shareholder formally sues, they often issue a 'books and records' demand to inspect corporate documents. Responding to those demands — legal review, document production — can run hundreds of thousands. The policy covers up to $500K of those costs. Good to have, especially given PE ownership.
findings.recommendation: Maintain.

findings.requirement_type: Hartford ML — Defense Within Retention Without Carrier Consent
findings.contract_quote: (Insured-favorable provision)
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #6 (PP 00 H112 00 0517): 'Insureds may settle a Claim entirely within the retention without insurer consent.'
findings.gap_description: Allows Insured to defend and settle small claims within the retention without carrier involvement. Speeds resolution of nuisance claims and avoids carrier control over small disputes.
findings.plain_english: For small claims that resolve under the $10,000 retention, you don't need to ask the carrier's permission to settle. Faster and quieter resolution of low-dollar disputes.
findings.recommendation: Maintain.

findings.requirement_type: Hartford ML — Personal Profit Exclusion Requires Final Adjudication
findings.contract_quote: (Insured-favorable language)
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #14 (PP 00 H363 00 0718): 'Personal profit exclusion now triggered only by judgment or non-appealable final adjudication. Carve-back for Securities Act §§11, 12, 15 violations.'
findings.gap_description: Personal profit / fraud exclusion triggered only by final non-appealable adjudication — meaning defense costs continue throughout litigation, only stopping if the insured is ultimately found guilty/liable in a final judgment. Insured-favorable.
findings.plain_english: If a director or officer is accused of fraud, the policy keeps paying defense costs through the entire case until there's a final, non-appealable judgment establishing the wrongdoing. Many policies cut off coverage on a mere allegation; this one doesn't. Critical for protecting the executive team.
findings.recommendation: Maintain.

findings.requirement_type: Hartford ML — Crime LLC Member Acts Exclusion (Operating Entity is LLC)
findings.contract_quote: (Internal control / fidelity exposure)
findings.policy_quote: Crime §V(B): 'Excludes loss from theft/deception fraud/forgery committed by partners or LLC members. As an LLC, Runbeck's LLC-member-perpetrated crime is excluded except limited carve-back for IA 1 (Employee Theft) and IA 2 (Forgery) subject to LLC-member-as-Employee paragraph (10) calculation.'
findings.gap_description: Run-Test's operating entity is an LLC (per Hartford ML named insured). LLC member theft/forgery is broadly excluded, with narrow carve-backs for Employee Theft and Forgery only when the member meets the policy's 'Employee' definition (paragraph 10 calculation). Members acting as members (not as employees) are excluded entirely.
findings.plain_english: Crime policies are designed for theft by 'employees,' but treat LLC owners differently — usually excluding theft by them. As an LLC, Runbeck's LLC members aren't fully covered if they commit fraud against the company. There are partial carve-backs, but only when the member is also acting as an employee. Worth understanding before relying on Crime as full insider-fraud protection.
findings.recommendation: (1) Confirm which individuals are LLC members vs employees. (2) For LLC members who actively work in the business, document their employee status and request the 'paragraph 10 LLC-member-as-Employee' calculation be applied. (3) At renewal, request a Member Theft endorsement that fully aligns LLC-member theft coverage with employee theft coverage. (4) Implement enhanced internal controls (segregation of duties, dual signatures) for executive-level transactions.
discoveryQuestions: Who are the LLC members of Runbeck Election Services LLC, and which of them are also employees with operational responsibilities?
If an LLC member misappropriated company funds, what's your understanding of how the Crime policy would respond?

findings.requirement_type: Hartford ML — Telephone & Toll Fraud 30-Day Loss Cap
findings.contract_quote: (Crime endorsement)
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #30 (PP 00 H672 00 0217): 'Loss capped to 30 consecutive days from discovery. Excludes losses from calling card / phone access card / phone credit card.'
findings.gap_description: Toll fraud capped at 30 days from first discovery. Slow-rolling toll fraud (international call routing through compromised PBX) typically isn't discovered until the next phone bill, which can be 30-60 days. The 30-day cap may exclude meaningful loss.
findings.plain_english: Phone-system hacking — where someone routes international calls through your phone system — is discovered when you get the phone bill. The policy only counts losses from the first 30 days of discovery, but the bill might not arrive for 60 days. This is a niche issue but worth noting.
findings.recommendation: Confirm phone system has fraud-detection alerts and monthly billing review. The 30-day cap is acceptable if discovery is quick. At renewal, evaluate whether to increase the 30-day window or remove cap.
discoveryQuestions: When does Run-Test review its phone system bills, and would unusually high international charges be flagged in real-time or after-the-fact?

findings.requirement_type: Cross-Program — Notice & Knowledge Endorsement (Hartford ML CEO/CFO Limited)
findings.contract_quote: (RMF Gen-4 — always-emit item)
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #10 (PP 00 H022 00 0616): 'Notice Manager limited to CEO and CFO of Named Entity. Narrows who can trigger notice obligations.'
findings.gap_description: On Hartford Management Liability, knowledge/notice obligations are limited to the CEO and CFO — preventing a low-level employee's awareness from being imputed to the entity. This is the broker-best-practice configuration.
findings.plain_english: On the management liability policy, only the CEO and CFO 'count' for purposes of notice obligations. So if a junior employee learns of a problem and doesn't escalate, that knowledge isn't automatically imputed to the company. This is exactly the configuration we want.
findings.recommendation: Maintain. Replicate this configuration on every other policy in the program (GL, Auto, Cyber, Umbrella, E&O) when those are placed (findings 1-5).

findings.requirement_type: Hartford ML — Manager Definition Includes Shadow Director (PE-Specific)
findings.contract_quote: (PE-backed entity protection)
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #9 (PP 00 H125 00 0718): 'Manager now includes de facto or shadow directors acting on behalf of Insured Entity with written indemnification agreement.'
findings.gap_description: Important for PE-backed companies. PE sponsor representatives who exercise control without holding formal director seats are explicitly covered as Managers if there's a written indemnification agreement.
findings.plain_english: PE sponsors often have representatives who influence the business without formally sitting on the board. This endorsement says they're covered too, as long as there's a written indemnification agreement in place.
findings.recommendation: Confirm with Lincoln Shields and Black Mountain that written indemnification agreements exist for any sponsor representatives exercising shadow-director influence. Without the indemnification agreement, the carve-back doesn't apply.

findings.requirement_type: Hartford ML — Subsidiary Definition Includes Controlled 501(c)(3)
findings.contract_quote: (Affiliate / charitable subsidiary protection)
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #11 (PP 00 H113 00 0517): 'Subsidiary now includes foundations, charitable trusts, PACs, or 501(c)(3) organizations controlled by Named Entity or Subsidiary.'
findings.gap_description: Extends D&O / EPL / Fiduciary to controlled charitable foundations and PACs. If Run-Test or its sponsors operate a charitable foundation or PAC, this provides automatic coverage.
findings.plain_english: If Run-Test or its owners operate a foundation, charity, or PAC, those entities also get D&O/EPL coverage automatically — no separate endorsement needed.
findings.recommendation: Confirm with the client whether any 501(c)(3), foundation, or PAC entities exist. Document them in the file even if covered automatically.

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento — Per-Project Aggregate (Construction-Only — Likely N/A)
findings.contract_quote: Contractors and Contractors engaged in other projects of construction shall have their general liability Aggregate Limit of Insurance endorsed to apply separately to each job site or project, as provided for by Insurance Services Office form CG-2503 ... (Sacramento §III.A)
findings.policy_quote: Per-Project Aggregate is a CGL endorsement (CG 25 03 / CG 25 04) — not applicable until GL is placed (finding-001). Sacramento clause expressly limited to 'projects of construction.'
findings.gap_description: Run-Test is an election services manufacturer, not a construction contractor. Per-Project Aggregate (CG 25 03 / CG 25 04) is a construction-industry endorsement and likely doesn't apply unless Run-Test performs physical construction at county sites. If Run-Test installs equipment at county elections offices (rack installations, mail-sorting equipment installs), Per-Location Aggregate (CG 25 04) may be more appropriate than Per-Project.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento has a per-project aggregate requirement, but it only applies to construction contractors. Run-Test isn't a construction company, so this doesn't apply to your business — unless you do physical equipment installation at county offices, in which case we'd want a per-location aggregate.
findings.recommendation: When GL is placed (finding-001), include CG 25 04 Per-Location Aggregate (covers each location separately) regardless of construction status — best practice for any multi-location operation. Verify with Sacramento whether installs at county sites are characterized as 'construction.'

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa — Auto Umbrella Attachment Ambiguity (Needs Review)
findings.contract_quote: Commercial/Business Automobile Liability insurance with a combined single limit ... of not less than $2,000,000 each occurrence ... (Maricopa §8.2.11). [Combined with §8.2.9] If available, the insurance policies required by this contract may be combined with Commercial Umbrella Insurance policies to meet the minimum limit requirements.
findings.policy_quote: (Interpretive question — no Auto policy or Umbrella policy is in this program submission per findings 2 and 5.)
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.9 has a program-level umbrella permission; §8.2.11 Auto clause does not inline-mention umbrella. CGL §8.2.10 explicitly does inline-mention umbrella. Strict reading: $2M Auto must be primary alone, not Auto-plus-Umbrella. Permissive reading: §8.2.9 program-level permission allows Umbrella to attach over $1M Auto. Recommend confirming with Maricopa County before treating Auto-plus-Umbrella as compliant. NOTE: this is a separate finding from finding-002 (no Auto policy) — the underlying Auto gap is its own Ugly finding regardless of how the umbrella ambiguity resolves.
findings.plain_english: When we eventually place Auto, we'll have a question: can a $1M Auto policy plus a $1M umbrella satisfy Maricopa's $2M Auto requirement? The contract is ambiguous. To stay safe, place Auto at $2M primary AND have an umbrella above it. Don't rely on the umbrella to fill the primary gap unless Maricopa explicitly approves.
findings.recommendation: (1) Place Auto at $2M CSL primary (per finding-002). (2) Place Umbrella at $10M+ over the $2M Auto (per finding-005). (3) If client cost-pressure pushes for $1M Auto + $1M Umbrella, request written confirmation from Maricopa County Risk Management before binding.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa — Cyber Claims-Made Retro Date Requirement
findings.contract_quote: In the event that the insurance required is written on a claims-made basis, Contractor warrants that any retroactive date under the policy shall precede the effective date of this contract and either continuous coverage will be maintained, or an extended discovery period will be exercised for a period of two years beginning at the time work under this contract is completed. (Maricopa §8.2.3)
findings.policy_quote: (No Cyber policy in program — finding-004.)
findings.gap_description: When Cyber is placed (per finding-004), the retro date must precede the original Maricopa contract effective date (11/01/2021 per the Maricopa contract analysis). Two-year ERP must be triggered if continuous coverage isn't maintained.
findings.plain_english: When we place the Cyber policy, the retro date — the date the carrier looks back to — needs to be on or before the date you started the Maricopa contract. Otherwise, if a breach happened years ago and is only now coming to light, it wouldn't be covered. We also need to make sure that if you ever switch carriers, you buy a 2-year tail.
findings.recommendation: When placing Cyber (finding-004) and any other claims-made policy: (1) retro date must precede 11/01/2021 (Maricopa contract effective date) at minimum, ideally to entity inception; (2) document continuous coverage at every renewal; (3) if the policy is non-renewed, immediately purchase 2-year ERP per Maricopa §8.2.3 (also Sacramento §V.A-C requires 1-year ERP).

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento — Civil Code §2782 Carve-Out (CA Public Policy)
findings.contract_quote: CIVIL CODE PROVISION: Coverage shall not extend to any indemnity coverage for the active negligence of the additional insured in any case where an agreement to indemnify the additional insured would be invalid under Subdivision (b) of Section 2782 of the Civil Code. (Sacramento §VII.B)
findings.policy_quote: (California public policy carve-out — no special endorsement required; satisfied by contract acknowledgement.)
findings.gap_description: Sacramento's clause carves AI coverage back to exclude indemnifying County for County's own active negligence — consistent with California public policy under Cal. Civ. Code §2782(b). This is a contract-level carve-back, not a policy endorsement requirement. Standard ISO CG 20 10 / CG 20 37 forms already align with §2782 limits.
findings.plain_english: California has a law that says you can't agree to insure another party against their own negligence. Sacramento's contract acknowledges this. Standard AI endorsements already comply. No specific action needed.
findings.recommendation: When GL is placed (finding-001), use ISO CG 20 10 + CG 20 37 (or equivalent broader-than-current-edition) — these forms align with §2782 limits.

findings.requirement_type: EPLI — Immigration Claim Coverage (Defense Costs Only, $100K Sublimit)
findings.contract_quote: (Operational risk — I-9 audit / immigration enforcement)
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #22 (PP 00 H430 00 0616): 'Sub-limit $100,000 (defense costs only — part of, not in addition to, EPLI aggregate). Retention $10,000. Prior/Pending 8/18/2023. Covers civil/criminal investigations re Immigration Control Act of 1986. Excludes labor/grievance arbitrations.'
findings.gap_description: Immigration claim is defense-cost-only at $100K sublimit (erodes EPLI aggregate). For a manufacturer with hourly labor potentially including immigrant workers, I-9 audits or ICE enforcement actions are real exposures. Defense costs only means no indemnity for fines, penalties, or settlements.
findings.plain_english: If ICE or USCIS audits Run-Test's I-9 records, the EPL policy will pay up to $100,000 in defense costs — and that money comes out of the main EPL limit, so it depletes coverage for other employment claims. There's no coverage for fines or penalties, only for legal defense.
findings.recommendation: Implement and document I-9 compliance program (E-Verify if appropriate, I-9 self-audit, retained immigration counsel on retainer). At renewal, evaluate whether to increase sublimit. If meaningful immigrant workforce, consider standalone Immigration Liability coverage.
discoveryQuestions: What does Run-Test's I-9 compliance look like — paper, electronic, E-Verify?
Have you ever had an ICE audit or USCIS site visit?
Do you use staffing agencies for production labor, and if so, do their employment screening protocols protect Run-Test from joint-employer liability?
